prompt: You're building a multiplayer game that sends each player's position 30 times a second. Why do many such games use UDP rather than TCP for position updates?

options.explanation: UDP has no encryption at all. Encryption comes from a layer on top (DTLS, QUIC or the game's own scheme).

options.text: UDP guarantees delivery faster than TCP
options.explanation: UDP guarantees nothing about delivery. It's attractive precisely because it doesn't try to deliver everything.

options.text: TCP can't send more than one message per second
options.explanation: TCP can carry very high message rates. The issue isn't throughput but head-of-line blocking and retransmission delay.

options.text: A lost update is superseded 33 ms later, so retransmitting it (and blocking newer updates behind it, as TCP would) only adds lag
options.explanation: Correct. TCP's in-order delivery would hold back fresh positions until a stale one is retransmitted. UDP lets the game drop the stale packet and use the newest state.

workedExample:
1. At 30 updates per second, a fresh position arrives roughly every 33 ms, and each one replaces the last.
2. With TCP, if one packet is lost, loss detection and retransmission take time, say tens of milliseconds. Meanwhile the next updates arrive, but TCP **can't deliver them** until the lost one is filled in, because it delivers bytes strictly in order.
3. Result: a visible stutter, all to deliver a position that is already out of date.
4. With UDP, the game simply uses the newest packet it has. Events that must not be lost (a kill, a purchase) can be sent with the game's own lightweight acknowledgements.

prompt: In HTTP/1.1, why did browsers open about six TCP connections per origin?

options.text: HTTP/1.1 closes the connection after every request
options.explanation: HTTP/1.1 made connections persistent by default (keep-alive). The limit is concurrency on a connection, not reuse.

options.text: Without HTTP/1.1 pipelining, each connection handles one request/response at a time, so parallel fetching needs more connections
options.explanation: Correct. Without working pipelining, a connection waits for each response to finish before the next can be sent; multiple connections are the only way to fetch resources concurrently.

options.text: Servers limited each connection to 100 KB
options.explanation: There's no such per-connection size limit in HTTP/1.1. Connections can carry arbitrarily large responses.

options.text: To provide redundancy in case one TCP connection drops
options.explanation: Redundancy isn't the reason. The six connections are for parallel fetching to work around HTTP-level head-of-line blocking.

workedExample:
1. A page needs, say, 60 resources.
2. Without working pipelining, one HTTP/1.1 connection carries one request and response at a time, so each resource waits at least one round trip behind the previous one.
3. Six connections let six requests be in flight at once, cutting that queue roughly six-fold, at the price of five extra handshakes and five separate slow starts.

HTTP/2 removes the reason: it can carry many concurrent requests on one connection, subject to stream limits and flow control. Completion time still depends on response size, server work, congestion and loss.
